demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
I remind myself it could have been worse
try hard not think about the trauma

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: Water/flooding triggers are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another in a car accident, given the rest of the profile centers on crash-related and guilt/shame themes. This trigger introduces a different threat context without support from memory or appraisal items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Feelings' is internally incoherent as worded: 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes the opposite of avoidance. Within the maladaptive strategies node, it directly conflicts with an avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'Body Unreliable' fits poorly with the rest of the profile for a perpetration-type accident trauma in which the patient's appraisals otherwise center on guilt, humiliation, and shattered beliefs. There are no memory, trigger, or strategy items suggesting bodily injury, panic/somatic threat, or physical incapacity to support this appraisal.

vignette:
Raj presented as a man carrying an immense, invisible weight. At forty-two, his work as a tax inspector demanded a meticulous attention to detail that he now struggled to maintain, his focus fractured by a single evening eight months prior. The event itself was a nightmarish collage of sensory fragments. He remembered the hypnotic sweep of the wipers against a relentless downpour, the glare of oncoming headlights on the wet asphalt, and then, with searing, unbearable clarity, the sound. It was not the screech of tires he replayed in his mind, but a sickening, dull thud, an acoustic signature of impact that would ambush him in the quiet of his office or in the dead of night. This sound was the most vivid piece of the memory; the moments immediately following it were a black hole. He knew he had gotten out of the car, knew he had seen the young woman on the ground, but he could not conjure the image. It was a blank space surrounded by the piercing auditory echo of his failure.

In the weeks that followed, Raj's world began to shrink. Driving, a necessity for his job, became an ordeal. The sight of any car pulled over, even for a minor fender-bender, would cause a surge of adrenaline, and the image of a crumpled bumper would flash behind his eyes. He started taking circuitous routes to avoid the intersection where the accident happened. His wife, Priya, noticed he no longer wanted to go for their customary Sunday drives. When she would try to talk about what happened, to bring it into the light, he would feel a cold panic. The subject was a door he had to keep bolted shut, certain that opening it would release something he couldn't control. He would try to force his mind onto other things, burying the intrusive thoughts under the dense, logical structures of the tax code. It was a constant, exhausting effort of suppression.

This internal battle was fueled by a profound sense of self-loathing. Raj had always believed he was a good, careful man who did the right thing. That belief had been annihilated on the wet pavement. Now, he was certain he was a monster hiding in plain sight, permanently marked by his carelessness. He felt a deep, unshakable humiliation, as if his failure was a brand on his forehead for all to see. In his darkest moments, he would tell himself that the anxiety, the sleepless nights, the intrusive sounds-they were all his deserved penance. He had failed to protect another human being, and for that, he should suffer. Occasionally, he would try to claw his way out by reminding himself that the woman had survived, that it could have been worse. But the thought provided no relief; it only highlighted the thin line between what did happen and an even more unthinkable outcome.

The consequences of his internal state began to bleed into his external life. When a colleague's father passed away, Raj called in sick for three days. The thought of attending the funeral, of being near a cemetery and the formal rituals of grief, was intolerable. It felt too close to the catastrophe he felt he had almost caused. His absence was noted, creating a distance between him and his work friends that he didn't know how to bridge. At home, his silence became a chasm between him and Priya. He saw the worry in her eyes but felt powerless to reassure her when he himself was so lost. It was Priya who finally insisted he seek help, telling him softly one evening, "I miss you, Raj. You're here, but you're not here." He came to therapy not because he believed he could be fixed, but because he was exhausted by the relentless effort of holding himself together. He was terrified that this state of torment was his new reality, a life sentence for a single, unforgivable moment.
